## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Vakajātaka* (Ja 300), translated as *The Wolf*, is a story in the canonical Pali Jātaka collection. According to its opening framework, the Buddha related the discourse while residing at Jetavana. The incident in the present concerns the elder Upasena, who had initially been rebuked for visiting the Buddha with an insufficiently trained junior companion; Upasena subsequently attained arahantship, undertook the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), and instructed other monks in them. After the Buddha granted permission for any monks observing these thirteen practices to visit him at will during his seclusion, other monks began adopting the practices insincerely solely for the sake of visiting, discarding their ascetic rags for clean robes as soon as the retreat concluded. Upon noticing the abandoned rags during an inspection of the monastery lodgings, the Buddha observed that their undertaking was transient, comparing it to a "wolf’s holy day service," and related the ancient tale.
